tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

# Licensing flags — resolve before shipping to an actual customer

Carried over from `RELEASE_ALPHA.md` §7 because this installer would put
both issues directly in a customer's hands, not just a developer's:

## ultralytics (AGPL-3.0)

`pose_pipeline` depends on `ultralytics` for YOLOv8 pose detection, and
`rigv4/studio/pose3d_studio.py`'s Process tab uses it too. AGPL-3.0 requires
that anything you distribute which incorporates it — or model weights
fine-tuned from it — makes its complete corresponding source available to
whoever receives it, including over a network. Shipping a closed-source
installer built on this without an Ultralytics Enterprise Licence is a
license violation, not just a risk.

Options, roughly in order of effort:
1. Buy an Ultralytics Enterprise Licence.
2. Swap the detection backend for a non-AGPL alternative (e.g. MediaPipe,
   which `pose3d_studio.py` already supports as a fallback path).
3. Ship this installer as source-available / AGPL-compliant.

Model weights (`yolov8m-pose.pt`) are **not** bundled in this installer on
purpose — `ultralytics` downloads them to its own cache on first run, so at
least the weights themselves aren't sitting in the installed tree.

## SMPL model files (non-commercial license)

`smplx` + SMPL body-mesh rendering (`smpl_fit.py`, `smpl_render.py`) is
**not** included in this installer's build (`build_installer.ps1` installs
only the `rig` and `pose` extras — not `smpl`). The SMPL model files
themselves are non-commercially licensed by their authors and were never
going to be bundled regardless of which extras are installed.

## Before you actually hand this to a customer

- [ ] Resolve the ultralytics question above.
- [ ] Confirm no SMPL-derived assets are anywhere in the runtime tree.
- [ ] Decide whether `pose_pipeline`'s dependency on `ultralytics`/`torch`
      (several GB) is worth it for the customer build, or whether that
      extra should be left out and sold as a separate add-on.

"""
pose_export_dataset.py -- turn corrected trials into a 2D pose training set.

The editor corrects 3D. A pose model learns 2D per image. Reprojecting the
corrected 3D into every calibrated camera bridges the two, and it is the whole
reason a multi-camera rig is worth annotating on: one manual correction
becomes N labelled images, and multi-view agreement gives an automatic quality
gate that single-image annotation cannot.

    python3 pose_export_dataset.py ~/offload/fuzhou_2_processed -o ~/datasets/lift_v1
    python3 pose_export_dataset.py ~/offload --recursive --dry-run

What it writes (COCO keypoints layout, because MMPose/RTMPose consume it
directly and it converts cleanly to the Ultralytics txt format):

    <out>/
        images/train/<session>__<trial>__<cam>__<frame>.jpg
        images/val/...
        annotations/train.json      COCO keypoints
        annotations/val.json
        dataset_meta.json           schema, gating settings, provenance counts

Design decisions worth knowing:

* **Splits are by trial, never by frame.** At 30fps consecutive frames are
  near-duplicates, so a random frame split leaks the validation set into
  training and reports a score that means nothing. Splitting whole trials (and
  ideally whole athletes -- pass --group-by to use a metadata field) is the
  only honest option.

* **Every label is gated.** A frame is exported only if the 3D it came from is
  trustworthy: manually keyed, or agreed on by enough cameras within a
  reprojection tolerance and with plausible segment lengths. Ungated
  auto-labels would just teach the model to reproduce its own errors.

* **Visibility is real.** A joint reprojecting inside the frame is not
  necessarily visible -- it may be behind the torso or the bar. Keypoints the
  detector had no confidence in are marked occluded (v=1) rather than visible
  (v=2), so the model is not trained to hallucinate what it cannot see.

* **Camera sync is applied.** Video frame indices are offset per camera (see
  pose_sync); exporting without that would pair a label with the wrong image,
  which is worse than not exporting at all.

* **Provenance is recorded per annotation** (`manual`, `n_cams`, `reproj_px`)
  so a later training run can weight hand-corrected labels above auto-gated
  ones, or drop the auto ones entirely.
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from typing import Dict, List

import cv2
import numpy as np

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))

## Current state
- 2026-11-03 (NODAL v0.2.1 inspected, not run): the Linux tarball (`https://github.com/NODAL3D/NODALCapture/releases/download/v0.2.1/NODAL-Setup-0.2.1-linux.tar.gz`, 720 MB) ships plain Python source in `NODAL-0.2.1/runtime/lib/python3.12/site-packages/{rigv4,pose_pipeline,gait_analysis}`. NODAL's own code has no license (all rights reserved): read it as a design, never copy it into BayCap. Facts: 2D detector is stock `yolov8m-pose.pt` (Ultralytics, AGPL-3.0, downloaded at first run) with MediaPipe as fallback; no NODAL-trained weights exist. `pose_pipeline/tracking/run.py` takes `--videos` plus an anipose/FreeMoCap `calibration.toml`. Their "fine tuning" is only a dataset exporter (`rigv4/studio/pose_export_dataset.py`): corrected 3D reprojected into every calibrated camera becomes COCO-keypoint labels; split by trial or athlete, never by frame; gate labels by camera count, reprojection error and segment-length plausibility; record provenance per label. Their `LICENSE_NOTICES.md` says their own AGPL issue is unresolved. Open, licensed equivalents for BayCap: anipose (BSD-2) or Pose2Sim (BSD-3) for calibration and triangulation, RTMPose/MMPose (Apache-2.0) for a fine-tunable 2D model. `rigv4` (camera control) needs NODAL hardware.

content.text:
**Short answer:** Yes, you can learn from it. You do not need to reverse engineer it. But there is nothing in it to fine-tune. And you cannot copy its code.

**What I found**
- The GitHub repo has only a README and the installers. The Linux installer holds plain Python code that anyone can read. I read it. I did not run it.
- **No license.** NODAL's own code has no license file. That means "all rights reserved." Read it for ideas. Do not paste it into BayCap.
- **No custom models.** The pose model is stock YOLOv8 from Ultralytics. MediaPipe is the backup. NODAL did not train any model of its own. So there is nothing of theirs to fine-tune.
- **Their "fine tuning" does not train anything.** It only exports a dataset. You fix the 3D pose one time. Then the code projects it into every camera view, so each fix gives you many labeled 2D images. Then you train an open model on those images.
- **The recipe is the useful part.** These rules from their code are worth using:
  - Split train and test by athlete or trial, not by frame.
  - Keep a label only if enough cameras agree on it.
  - Record where each label came from.
- **Their own license notes say they have an open license problem.** YOLO uses AGPL, a license that makes you share your source code if you hand the software to others. NODAL has not fixed this yet.
- **Their capture code needs NODAL cameras.** It is no use with iPhones.

**What fits your BayCap project**
Build the same pipeline from open tools that have real licenses:
- anipose or Pose2Sim: calibrate the cameras and build 3D. NODAL uses the same calibration file format that anipose uses.
- RTMPose: a 2D pose model you can fine-tune on Baylor athlete video. It uses the Apache license, so it has no AGPL problem.
- Then we write our own version of NODAL's label exporter.

I put all of this in BayCap's status file. I also fixed two wrong lines there: the folder path and the GitHub repo name. Commit `47b48d2` is pushed to `erash11/fp-baycap`.

**What you do now:** nothing. BayCap is still parked. The next BayCap step is still OpenCap setup and a test CMJ recording. Fine-tuning comes after you have recorded multi-camera sessions to label.

Not checked: I did not install or test anipose, Pose2Sim or RTMPose. The 720 MB download is in this job's temp folder, and it is deleted when the job ends.
